analysis.one_liner: Phases in a national requirement that all new passenger cars sold be zero-emission by 2035.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final three weeks of the 117th Congress with 18 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the EPA to set a national zero-emission vehicle standard. Starting with model year 2026, car manufacturers would have to ensure a rising share of the new cars they deliver for sale are zero-emission — 35% in 2026, climbing each year to 100% in 2035. After 2035, manufacturers could sell only zero-emission passenger vehicles. Companies that fall short could buy credits from companies that exceed the targets, or pay a civil penalty set at twice the value of the missing credits, with penalty money going to the Highway Trust Fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit through lower tailpipe pollution — smog-forming and climate emissions from new cars would be phased out nationwide. Over time, drivers shift to vehicles that cost less to fuel and maintain. Manufacturers that already sell zero-emission vehicles gain a new revenue stream: they earn one credit per zero-emission vehicle delivered and can sell or trade surplus credits to companies falling short.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities breathing car exhaust, and EV makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a mandatory national schedule — 35% zero-emission sales in model year 2026 rising to 100% by model year 2035 — so new-car tailpipe pollution is phased out nationwide rather than left to state-by-state rules.
After model year 2035, the EPA must issue injunctions barring manufacture of any passenger vehicle other than a zero-emission vehicle, locking in the endpoint.

Civil penalties for noncompliance — set at twice the value of the credits a manufacturer failed to submit — are deposited into the Highway Trust Fund, so enforcement revenue goes back into roads and transit.
The bill preserves states' authority to set their own stricter emissions and zero-emission vehicle rules, so states like California could keep going further.

analysis.who_pays: Legacy automakers that sell mostly gasoline vehicles bear the compliance costs: they must hit the escalating sales percentages, buy credits from competitors, or pay civil penalties. Consumers could face higher upfront prices for new vehicles during the transition, and the bill's credit-trading system lets well-financed laggards pay their way out of actually changing their product lines. Gasoline producers and retailers face shrinking long-term demand for their product.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas-car automakers, consumers at the showroom, oil industry

drawbacks.text: The escalating mandates could raise the upfront price of a new car in the 2026–2035 window, hitting hardest in years when zero-emission models are still more expensive to build and when lower-income buyers dominate the new-car market's cheapest segment.

The bill allows credits to be sold, transferred, and traded, and lets the EPA delegate administration of the trading market to a private market-making entity — a structure that lets manufacturers with money buy compliance instead of selling cleaner cars, and creates a valuable new financial market out of a regulatory obligation.

The bill offers only a nonbinding 'sense of Congress' that manufacturers should diversify vehicle technologies and models to ensure consumer choice and access — it sets no requirement on vehicle price, affordability, or model variety, leaving affordability and access concerns unaddressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is real: a binding national phase-out of new gas-car sales by 2035 delivers cleaner air and lower fuel costs over time, at the price of higher compliance costs for automakers and likely higher new-car prices during the transition. The design has genuine weaknesses — a tradable credit market that lets deep-pocketed laggards buy compliance, and no binding affordability or consumer-access provisions — but the mandate itself has teeth, with defined percentages, civil penalties, and a 2035 injunction on new gas-car manufacturing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 14, 2022 and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended three weeks later.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Levin (D-CA) introduced the Zero-Emission Vehicles Act of 2022 in the House on December 14, 2022, with 15 original cosponsors joining at introduction.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which was its only committee assignment.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — was ever taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, which by itself killed the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers that sell gasoline vehicles are better off: they face no compliance schedule, no credit purchases, no civil penalties, and no 2035 manufacturing ban. Gasoline demand continues on its existing path, and credit-revenue prospects for EV-leading manufacturers never materialized from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gas-car automakers, with no new rules

for.name: Rep. Mike Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 14, 2022 and assembled 15 original cosponsors.

for.name: 18 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 18 cosponsors were Democrats and none was a Republican.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce (Chair Frank Pallone)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 14, 2022 and took no further action — no hearing or markup — for the remaining three weeks of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican supported the bill, and it died in a Democratic-chaired committee without either party moving it.

industries.note: The bill would force an escalating share of their new-car sales to be zero-emission from 2026, reaching 100% in 2035, with civil penalties at twice the value of missing credits and an injunction on gas-car manufacturing thereafter. Their cost of compliance is the source of the cleaner air and lower fuel costs the public gains.

Makers of electric and fuel-cell vehicles earn one credit per vehicle delivered and can sell, transfer, or trade surplus credits to lagging competitors, creating a new revenue stream. They profit from the same mandate that cuts the public's tailpipe pollution exposure.

A 2035 endpoint for new gas-car sales steadily erodes long-term gasoline demand. The industry's interest in continued gasoline sales runs against the air-quality and climate benefits the bill targets.

The bill authorizes a national tradeable credit market, possibly administered by a private market-making entity, turning the compliance obligation into a financial instrument. Compliance could be bought rather than achieved, though annual public reporting on the market is required.
